title: Complexity & Big-O
tagline: The language interviewers use to compare solutions.
intro:
Big-O notation is the shared language interviewers use to judge whether your solution is good. It answers one question: **as the input grows, how fast does the work grow?** Not how many milliseconds it takes on your laptop — that depends on hardware — but the *shape* of the growth curve as n heads toward infinity.

Every coding interview ends with the same exchange: "What's the time and space complexity?" If you can't answer crisply, even a correct solution looks junior. If you can — and can explain *why* — you signal the engineering maturity that gets offers.

This module gives you the complexity ladder (the handful of growth rates that cover ~99% of interviews), a reliable procedure for reading complexity straight off your code, the often-missed ideas of amortised and space complexity, and the exact sentence to say out loud when asked.
objectives: Define Big-O, Big-Theta, and Big-Omega and explain which one interviews actually mean
Rank the complexity ladder from O(1) to O(n!) and recognise each from code
Derive time complexity by counting nested loops and recursive branching
Explain amortised analysis (why dynamic-array append is O(1), not O(n))
Analyse space complexity, including the hidden cost of the recursion call stack
State complexity in one clean interview sentence and justify the dominant term

signals: Any time you finish a solution — always state time AND space
"Can you do better?" — they want a lower complexity class
Comparing two candidate approaches before coding
Choosing a data structure (the operations' costs decide it)
antiSignals: Don't micro-optimise constants (O(2n) and O(n) are the same class)
Don't quote best-case to dodge a bad average/worst case
Don't confuse 'it ran fast' with 'low complexity' — n may be small

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Big-O is just a way of asking 'if the input gets bigger, how much more work do I do?' - not how many seconds it takes on your laptop. Think of cooking for guests: if 1 guest takes 1 step and 10 guests take 10 steps, the work grows in a straight line. But if every guest must shake hands with every other guest, the work grows much faster.

Example: finding a name by flipping a phone book page by page grows with its size - double the pages, double the flips. But opening to the middle and always throwing away half the book finds the name in only a handful of steps. Same goal, wildly different growth - and that difference is exactly what Big-O measures.

sections.heading: Core definitions — the vocabulary
sections.body:
Three Greek-letter bounds exist, but interviews almost always mean Big-O describing the worst case.

| Term | Bounds | Plain meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Big-O** `O(f)` | Upper bound | Grows *no faster than* f. "Worst case." |
| **Big-Omega** `Ω(f)` | Lower bound | Grows *at least* as fast as f. "Best case." |
| **Big-Theta** `Θ(f)` | Tight bound | Grows *exactly* like f (upper = lower). |
| **Amortised** | Average over a sequence | Cost *per operation* across many operations. |

Two rules collapse messy expressions into a clean class: **drop constants** (O(2n) → O(n)) and **keep only the dominant term** (O(n² + n) → O(n²)). Complexity is about the *limit* as n → ∞, where the biggest term swamps everything else.

callouts.text: When someone says "the complexity is O(n)" they almost always mean the *tight worst-case* bound. Use Big-O unless explicitly asked for best or average case.

sections.heading: The complexity ladder
sections.body:
Sorted from fastest-growing-slowest to explosive. Memorise this order — it's the y-axis interviewers picture.

| Class | Name | Doubling n does this | Typical source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O(1) | Constant | nothing | hash lookup, array index |
| O(log n) | Logarithmic | +1 step | binary search, balanced BST |
| O(n) | Linear | doubles | single loop / scan |
| O(n log n) | Linearithmic | a bit more than doubles | good sorts, divide & conquer |
| O(n²) | Quadratic | ×4 | nested loops over the same input |
| O(2^n) | Exponential | squares | subsets, naive recursion |
| O(n!) | Factorial | explodes | permutations, brute-force TSP |

The jump from O(n log n) to O(n²) is the line most "can you do better?" questions are about. Anything O(2^n) or worse is only acceptable when n is tiny (n ≤ ~20).

callouts.text: Rule of thumb at n = 10^6: O(n) and O(n log n) are fine, O(n²) is far too slow (~10^12 ops). If n ≤ ~20, exponential is acceptable.

sections.heading: How to read complexity off your code
sections.body:
You rarely need formal math. This procedure handles almost every interview problem.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Look at the code"] --> B{"Loops over input?"}
  B -- "No loop, fixed work" --> C["O(1)"]
  B -- "One loop" --> D["O(n)"]
  B -- "Nested loops over same n" --> E["O(n^2)"]
  B -- "Halve the range each step" --> F["O(log n)"]
  B -- "Loop + sort inside" --> G["O(n log n)"]
  A --> H{"Recursive?"}
  H -- "branches^depth" --> I["O(branches^depth) e.g. 2^n"]
```

For recursion, the shortcut is **(number of branches) ^ (depth of recursion)**, adjusted by memoisation. Computing Fibonacci naively branches twice per call to depth n → O(2^n); memoising collapses it to O(n).

sections.heading: Amortised analysis — the one people miss
sections.body:
A dynamic array (Java `ArrayList`, Python `list`) appends in **amortised O(1)**, even though an occasional append triggers an O(n) resize-and-copy. Why? Because the array doubles its capacity, those expensive resizes happen rarely enough that the *average* cost per append, spread across n appends, is constant.

Think of it like a phone plan: a few big bills (resizes) averaged over many cheap months (normal appends) gives a low monthly cost. Interviewers love when you say "append is amortised O(1)" rather than incorrectly calling it O(n).

callouts.text: Amortised O(1) is NOT the same as worst-case O(1). A single append can still be O(n) — it's the *average over the sequence* that is constant.

sections.heading: Space complexity (don't forget the call stack)
sections.body:
Space complexity counts **extra** memory your algorithm allocates beyond the input. The output usually doesn't count unless the problem treats it as working memory.

The most-missed source of space is the **recursion call stack**: each pending recursive call holds a frame. A recursion that goes n deep is O(n) space even if it allocates nothing else. A balanced-tree DFS is O(log n) stack; a skewed tree (or linked-list recursion) is O(n) stack and can overflow.

| Pattern | Extra space |
| --- | --- |
| In-place swap / two pointers | O(1) |
| Hash map of seen values | O(n) |
| Recursion depth d | O(d) stack |
| 2-D DP table | O(n·m) |
| 1-D DP after compression | O(n) |

sections.heading: Stating complexity in the interview
sections.body:
End every solution with a single, confident sentence in this shape: **"This is O(⟨time⟩) time because ⟨dominant work⟩, and O(⟨space⟩) space because ⟨what I allocate⟩."**

Examples:

- "O(n) time — one pass over the array — and O(n) space for the hash map."
- "O(n log n) time, dominated by the sort, and O(1) extra space since I sort in place."
- "O(2^n) time because I branch on include/exclude at each element, and O(n) space for the recursion depth."

Always name the *dominant term* and *why* it dominates. That 'why' is the signal.

interviewTalking: Treat the complexity statement as part of the solution, not an afterthought. The moment you finish coding, say: "Let me give you the complexity." Then state time and space in one sentence each, naming the dominant operation. If they ask "can you do better?", they're telling you a lower complexity class exists — usually it means replacing a nested loop (O(n²)) with hashing (O(n)) or sorting (O(n log n)), or replacing a linear scan (O(n)) with binary search (O(log n)).
commonMistakes: Quoting best-case (Ω) when the interviewer wants worst-case (O) — e.g. calling quicksort 'O(n log n)' without noting O(n²) worst case
Forgetting the recursion call stack counts as space
Keeping non-dominant terms (saying O(n² + n) instead of O(n²))
Keeping constants (saying O(2n) instead of O(n))
Calling dynamic-array append O(n) instead of amortised O(1)
Confusing 'fast on my input' with 'low complexity' — small n hides a bad class
complexityNotes: Big-O describes asymptotic growth as n → ∞, ignoring constants and lower-order terms. Interview answers should give the tight worst-case time and the extra (auxiliary) space, always naming the dominant term and the reason it dominates.
